P1.evidence: P1a is a costly miss here. The setter had spoken to him that same day and the rep read nothing back, so the prospect had to supply it himself — 'yeah, I spoke with Kim earlier today' — and, crucially, the rep did not know that Jacob had already decided to buy the $200 product and was only on the call because Kim had routed him. That single piece of setter context would have changed the entire call. The two-part frame ran with 'if that's cool with you' as the agreement check, and the open question ran cleanly.

P2.evidence: Age was asked ('I don't know how old you are' — 28) but height, weight and body composition never were. Work ran properly — 'Do you work? I presume you work, right?' then 'What do you do?' — producing the life coaching, breathwork and caregiving picture that the rep then used well in Phase 3. Health conditions and injuries were never asked; the prospect volunteered 'I don't have any pain in my body. I feel good overall', which is the one call in this batch where that answer would have been reassuring had anyone sought it. Diet, sleep and results were untouched.

P3.evidence: Strong work against an unusually difficult case — a prospect with no pain and no problem. The rep refused three thin answers in a row: 'Why? What did say? Why?', then 'what's the importance of this way of training for your body, for your life? Tell me more', then 'I'm still trying to understand, like, by you implementing this into your life, like, what does that yield for you?' and finally 'how do you want to show up in you as you enter your 30s?' The 1-10 potential scale returned a seven with a good reason attached. P3f ran systematically — partner, then business, then back to the partner — and produced the real driver: credibility as a coach, 'it sends a message that they're in control of themselves, and definitely increases people's desire to hear what you have to say.'

P4.evidence: Entirely absent. Nothing was asked about what he has tried, what happened, why it did not stick, or what is in the way. P4f matters most and is the direct cause of the commercial outcome: this prospect assembles his own training and was choosing between a $200 self-serve course and one-to-one coaching. 'The information isn't the problem, so why can't you stick to it on your own?' is the question that separates those two products, and it was never asked. Partially excusable — he has no failure history to mine — but the phase still had a job to do here and did not do it.

P5.evidence: No consequence frame. The want-or-need question ran and returned 'I'd say both', but the follow-up dissolved it rather than sharpening it — the prospect said 'I'm at peace where I am now' and the rep accepted that and closed the phase with 'yes, don't really need to ask any other questions. As you said, you're not in any pain.' Nothing established a cost of inaction, which for an optimizer is the whole job.

P6.evidence: The 1-10 athletic potential scale ran and was followed by 'Do you want to get to that 10 out of 10?' — 'Yeah.' That is a commitment of sorts but not P6a's question about believing he can get there with the right structure and the right person, which is exactly the belief that justifies coaching over a course. P6b never ran. The prospect then raised the money question himself before any commitment had been banked.

P11.evidence: Scored against the product actually sold, a $200/month self-serve subscription, not the coaching programme. Payment was collected and confirmed live — 'It says like I got a receipt, so I'm good to go' — with the rep staying on the call specifically to verify onboarding, which is good practice: 'I'll make sure you just, whilst I'm here, you know, you're onboarded correctly, because there could be some hiccups.' No Trevor call and no agreement apply to this product. He was walked into the Skool app and access confirmed, but no welcome email or onboarding questionnaire was mentioned.

objection_plays.detail: A money signal arrived — 'investing in one-on-one coaching may not be the move right now' — accompanied by an explicit invitation to pitch anyway: 'I'm open to hearing, too, what the one-on-one looks like.' Not one OC move ran. No isolate, no 'you're not in a SHOULD I place, you're in a HOW place', no payment-plan mention, no permission question, no financial picture. The rep did not merely fail to work the objection, he agreed with it and argued against his own offer: 'One-on-one coaching from the sounds of it. I'm not sure if it will. This, on the other hand, probably is.' The coaching price was never spoken aloud on this call.

Worth recording as a script gap rather than a rep failure: there is no scripted play for a prospect who arrives already intending to buy the low-tier product and is routed to a closer anyway. Jacob said it plainly — 'I was planning on joining this one today, and then I got a call from Kim... But I was already ready to go to sign up with this.' The process has no move for converting a self-serve buyer upward, and no rule for when a closer should decline the call. Twenty-eight minutes of closer time produced revenue that was already inbound.

notes: Phase 3 was genuinely skilful — extracting a buying reason from a man with no pain, no injuries and nothing wrong is the hardest version of that phase and the rep did it, landing on professional credibility as the real driver. Everything downstream then went unused. Phase 4 never ran, so the one question that distinguishes coaching from a course was never asked; Phase 5 never ran, so there was no cost of inaction; and when the money signal came the rep argued for the cheaper product before ever quoting the more expensive one. The prospect explicitly asked to hear about the coaching and did not. Two coaching points: read the setter notes before the call, and never talk a prospect out of an offer he has just invited you to present.
